summary.en: A civil war in 1967–1970 between Nigeria and Biafra, the breakaway state declared by the Eastern Region, with the Igbo people as its largest group. Nigeria surrounded and blockaded Biafra, and the blockade led to a famine in which hundreds of thousands of civilians died, most of them children and women. The war was one of the first to be shown on television around the world.

text.en: Wikipedia and Wikidata give 6 July 1967–15 January 1970. UCDP gives the same start but says that the fighting ceased on 12 January 1970, and Wikipedia writes that the surrender was signed on 14 January in Lagos.

intro.en: Nigeria became independent from Britain in 1960 as a federation with deep divisions between the regions and ethnic groups. In January 1966 young officers, most of the known planners being Igbo, killed several leading politicians in a coup, among them the prime minister and the premiers of the Northern and Western Regions. In July 1966 northern soldiers carried out a counter-coup, and Yakubu Gowon took power. From June to October 1966 an estimated 10,000–30,000 Igbo were killed in pogroms in northern Nigeria, half of them children, and one to two million fled to the Eastern Region. An eyewitness, the ethnomusicologist Charles Keil, described how the army led the massacres in town after town. At negotiations in Aburi in Ghana the Eastern Region's military governor Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu and Gowon agreed on a looser federation, but Gowon did not keep the agreement. On 27 May 1967 Gowon divided the country into twelve states, so that the Igbo would lose control of most of the oil, and on 30 May Ojukwu proclaimed the Republic of Biafra. Nigeria responded with a blockade, and on 6 July 1967 federal troops attacked in what was called a police action.

members.en: The federal military government under General Yakubu Gowon, with commanders such as Murtala Mohammed, Benjamin Adekunle and Olusegun Obasanjo. The army grew from about 7,000 to 200,000 men. Britain and the Soviet Union supplied weapons, and the British weapons were, according to the source, the most important factor in the outcome of the war. Egypt sent bombers with their own crews.

The Republic of Biafra under Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu and from January 1970 Philip Effiong. Only five countries recognised Biafra: Tanzania, Gabon, Ivory Coast, Zambia and Haiti. Biafra received weapons from France, which denied it, and hired foreign mercenaries, among them the Swede Carl Gustaf von Rosen, who led small air raids and flew in food and medicine. About 40 per cent of Biafra's population belonged to peoples other than the Igbo, for example the Ibibio, Ijaw and Ogoni, and many of them suffered abuses from both sides.

outcome.en: Nigeria won. During the final offensive in January 1970 Ojukwu fled to Ivory Coast, and his successor Philip Effiong surrendered. Biafra ceased to exist and Nigeria was united again. Gowon spoke of national reconciliation, but many Igbo have since felt politically and economically excluded, and new Biafran movements have emerged. The images of starving children attracted great attention around the world from the middle of 1968. French doctors who had worked in Biafra, among them Bernard Kouchner, formed a group that in 1971 became Médecins Sans Frontières. The blockade also contributed to starvation as a method of warfare being prohibited in the Additional Protocols to the Geneva Conventions in 1977. Whether what happened was a genocide is disputed among scholars.

casualties.en: The death tolls are very uncertain and disputed. According to the source's compilation, 45,000–100,000 soldiers were killed, about 100,000 according to another figure. Estimates of civilians who died of starvation and disease during the blockade range from about 500,000 to 2 or 3 million according to the article on the war, and up to 4 million according to the article on the blockade; it also says that one million or more died. Most were children and women. The International Committee of the Red Cross estimated in September 1968 that 8,000–10,000 people died of starvation every day. Nigerian leaders said openly that starvation was a weapon in the war. Federal troops are also accused of bombing civilians, massacres and rapes, among other places in Asaba, and Biafran forces of abuses against minority peoples suspected of sabotage. Two to four and a half million people were driven from their homes. The UCDP research programme at Uppsala University counts the conflict between Nigeria's government and Biafra as a war (at least 1,000 battle-related deaths per year) in every year 1967–1970, but has no death figures for these years.

summary.en: On 30 May 1967, three days after Gowon divided the Eastern Region into three states, the military governor Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu declares the region independent as the Republic of Biafra. Behind the decision lie the pogroms against the Igbo in the north in 1966 and the belief that the federal government did not want to or could not protect them. Nigeria immediately imposes a blockade on all shipping to Biafra except oil tankers, and soon on those as well.

On 4 October 1967 Nigeria's 1st Division captures Biafra's capital Enugu. Ojukwu, who is sleeping in the government building when the attack comes, escapes disguised as a servant. Nigeria hopes that the leaders of the Igbo people will now give up the fight for independence, but this does not happen: Ojukwu moves the government to Umuahia, deep inside Igbo territory, and the war continues.

text.en: The event has no entry of its own in Wikidata that could be compared. The date comes from Wikipedia's article on the war, and the article on Operation Tail-Wind gives October 1967. The point shows the city of Enugu according to Wikidata.

summary.en: When Nigeria's 2nd Division under Murtala Mohammed captures Asaba in October 1967, the soldiers kill Igbo civilians in the town. On 7 October the residents gather for a peaceful procession in support of a united Nigeria, but the soldiers separate out men and boys and shoot them with machine guns. Estimates range from 500 to over 1,000 dead; the researchers Bird and Ottanelli give 500–800.

Nigeria closes Biafra's ports, airfields, mail and trade, and the blockade is maintained for two and a half years. The most important source of protein, dried fish from Norway, disappears, and the children suffer from starvation and the deficiency disease kwashiorkor. From the middle of 1968 people around the world see the images of starving children, and aid organisations fly in food in the Biafran airlift. At least half a million civilians die, according to several estimates considerably more.

text.en: Wikidata has an entry on the blockade but gives no time. The information comes from Wikipedia's articles on the war and on the blockade, which give very different numbers of dead (from 500,000 to 4 million).

caption.en: Aid workers unload boxes of dried fish flown in from Calabar or Port Harcourt, for refugee camps outside the war zone during the civil war in Nigeria and Biafra. Photograph by Lyle Conrad, CDC, 1968. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 19 May 1968 Benjamin Adekunle's troops capture the port city of Port Harcourt. Biafra has already lost Enugu, Bonny and Calabar, and the ring around Biafra is closed. Oil production starts up again, and the oil money gives Nigeria the means to buy more weapons, something Biafra cannot match.

text.en: The event has no entry of its own in Wikidata. The date appears in two Wikipedia articles, on the war and on Operation Tail-Wind.

summary.en: On 7 January 1970 Olusegun Obasanjo's 3rd Marine Commando Division launches the final offensive. Owerri falls on 9 January and Uli, with Biafra's airfield, on 11 January. Ojukwu flies into exile in Ivory Coast and hands over to Philip Effiong, who surrenders on 13 January. The surrender is signed in Lagos, and on 15 January 1970 the war is over.

text.en: Wikipedia and Wikidata date the operation to 7–12 January 1970. The article on the operation gives both 8 and 9 January for Ojukwu's flight. The accounts of the surrender differ: to Obasanjo on 13 January according to the article on the operation, to Gowon on 13 January and signed in Lagos on 14 January according to the article on the war.

summary.en: The war between Israel and a coalition of Arab states began the day after Israel was proclaimed, on 15 May 1948, and ended with the armistice agreements of 1949. In Israel the war is called the War of Independence. For the Palestinians it is part of the Nakba, “the catastrophe”, when over 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled.

intro.en: After the Balfour Declaration in 1917 and the British Mandate for Palestine in 1920, tensions grew between Arabs, Jews and the British, along with Zionism and the large Jewish immigration from Europe. On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly voted for a partition plan: an Arab state on about 43 per cent of the Mandate, a Jewish state on 56 per cent, although the Jews were a third of the population, and Jerusalem under international administration. The Jewish leaders accepted the plan, but the Palestinian and other Arab leaders did not. A civil war broke out, and in April 1948 Zionist forces began to conquer and empty towns and villages according to Plan Dalet. On 14 May 1948 the State of Israel was proclaimed, and the next morning Egypt, Transjordan, Syria and Iraqi forces entered Palestine.

members.en: The Haganah with the Palmach, the Irgun and Lehi, from 26 May 1948 the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), as well as Druze and Bedouin groups and foreign volunteers (Mahal).

name.en: The Arab League states and Palestinian forces

members.en: Egypt, Transjordan, Iraq and Syria, with smaller forces from Saudi Arabia and Yemen. Lebanon took part in only one battle. In addition there were Palestinian and other volunteer forces, among them the Arab Liberation Army and the Army of the Holy War.

outcome.en: After the war Israel controlled about 78 per cent of the former Mandate, including West Jerusalem. Transjordan took East Jerusalem and the West Bank, which it annexed the following year, and Egypt occupied the Gaza Strip. The 1949 armistice agreements drew the Green Line. Over 700,000 Palestinians had fled or been expelled, which became the beginning of the Palestinian refugee problem. Over the following three years about as many Jews moved, fled or were expelled from the Arab countries, and 260,000 of them came to Israel. The war is called the War of Independence in Israel and the Nakba by the Palestinians. The concept of the 1948 Palestine war also includes the civil war from November 1947.

casualties.en: On the Israeli side about 6,373 died according to the historian Stanley Sandler (about 4,000 soldiers and 2,400 civilians); Benny Morris gives 5,700–5,800. The Arab states' armies lost an estimated 3,700–7,000 dead, and among the Palestinians 3,000–13,000 soldiers and civilians died (Aref al-Aref gives 13,000, most of them civilians). The figures are estimates and differ.

summary.en: On 14 May 1948, the same day the British Mandate ends, David Ben-Gurion proclaims the State of Israel at the Tel Aviv Museum. The next morning armies from Egypt, Transjordan, Syria and Iraq enter Palestine. In Israel the day is celebrated as Independence Day, while the Palestinians see it as the beginning of the Nakba.

text.en: Wikipedia and Wikidata give the same date, 14 May 1948, for the declaration of independence. Wikidata's coordinates for the declaration, however, do not lie in Tel Aviv, so the point is Tel Aviv according to Wikidata.

caption.en: David Ben-Gurion reads the declaration of independence in Tel Aviv on 14 May 1948, beneath a portrait of Theodor Herzl. Photograph by Rudi Weissenstein. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Latrun lay on the only road between Jewish-held Jerusalem and the rest of Israel. Israel's forces attacked the Jordanian Arab Legion there five times between May and July 1948 but could not take the place, which remained Jordanian until the Six-Day War in 1967.

text.en: Wikipedia's infobox and Wikidata state that the fighting began on 24 May 1948, while the article's introduction writes 25 May.

summary.en: In July 1948 the Israel Defense Forces conquer the Palestinian towns of Lydda and Ramle, and 50,000–70,000 inhabitants are forcibly expelled. Hundreds of Palestinians are killed, among other things in the Lydda massacre and during what is called the Lydda death march. It was the largest expulsion of the war and a part of the Nakba. The towns, which under the UN partition plan would have belonged to the Arab state, became part of Israel.

On 15–22 October 1948 Israeli forces under Yigal Allon attack the Egyptian forces in the Negev. The aim was to separate the Egyptian units on the coast from those along the road Beersheba–Hebron–Jerusalem, and in the longer term to conquer the whole Negev.

After negotiations on Rhodes, which began in January, Egypt and Israel sign an armistice agreement on 24 February 1949. Later the same year Israel also concluded agreements with Lebanon, Transjordan and Syria. The agreements drew the Green Line, which according to the text was not to be seen as a political border.

text.en: Wikidata has only one joint entry for all the 1949 armistice agreements, with the year but without date and place, so the agreement with Egypt could not be compared with a second source.

summary.en: On 5–10 March 1949 Israeli brigades take the southern Negev down to the Red Sea, an area that Jordan claimed in the armistice negotiations. They met no major resistance. The name means “fact” in Hebrew. It was the last campaign of the war.

On 5–10 June 1967 Israel fought a coalition of Arab states, mainly Egypt, Syria and Jordan. Israel conquered and occupied the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank with East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights. The war is also called the 1967 Arab–Israeli War, and many of its consequences are still unresolved.

text.en: How many Palestinians were displaced is given differently in Wikipedia's article: 280,000–325,000 in the text and 413,000 in the infobox. The war and its dates, 5–10 June 1967, agree with Wikidata.

intro.en: After the Suez Crisis in 1956 a UN force (UNEF) stood in Sinai to ensure that the armistice of 1949 was kept. There were nevertheless frequent border clashes, especially with Syria, and a growing pan-Arab nationalism that wanted to unite the Arab countries against Israel. In April 1967 Israel shot down six Syrian aircraft in a border incident, and the Soviet Union gave false information that Israel was massing troops against Syria. In mid-May Egypt's president Gamal Abdel Nasser moved 100,000 soldiers to the border and demanded that the UN force leave the area. He then closed the Straits of Tiran, Israel's only route to the Red Sea, to Israeli ships; Israel had said that this would count as an act of war. Egypt concluded defence pacts with Syria and Jordan, and Iraqi troops entered Jordan. On 4 June Israel's government decided to go to war, and the next morning Israel attacked Egypt's airfields.

members.en: Egypt, Syria and Jordan, with Iraqi forces and minor involvement by Lebanon. Saudi troops were moved to Jordan during the war.

outcome.en: Egypt and Jordan accepted a ceasefire on 8 June and Syria on 9 June, and it was signed on 11 June. By then Israel had occupied the Golan Heights, the West Bank with East Jerusalem, the Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza Strip, and about one million Arabs came under Israeli rule. About 280,000–325,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from the West Bank and Gaza, something called the Naksa (“the setback”) in Arabic, and about 100,000 Syrians left the Golan Heights. Egypt closed the Suez Canal in 1967–1975. The name Six-Day War was chosen in Israel by Yitzhak Rabin. In November 1967 the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 242 on peace and on Israel withdrawing from territories occupied in the war.

casualties.en: In total over 15,000 Arabs and fewer than 1,000 Israelis died. On the Israeli side 776–983 died (Gawrych). Egypt lost 9,800–15,000 dead or missing (Herzog), Syria 1,000–2,500 dead (Tucker) and Jordan about 700 (Gawrych). In addition 20 Israeli civilians were killed in Jerusalem, 15 UN soldiers in Sinai and 34 Americans when Israel mistakenly attacked the ship USS Liberty. The figures are estimates and are given as ranges.

summary.en: At 07:45 on 5 June 1967 Israel's air force attacks Egypt's air bases and destroys most of Egypt's air force on the ground. After Syrian and Jordanian counter-attacks their air bases are bombed too. By midday about 450 Egyptian, Jordanian and Syrian aircraft were destroyed, and Israel had air supremacy for the rest of the war.

caption.en: Egyptian aircraft destroyed on the ground at an air base, June 1967. Photographer unknown. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: On 5–6 June 1967 an Israeli division under Ariel Sharon takes the crossroads at Abu-Ageila in Sinai from the Egyptian army. The defeat opened the way into Sinai, and Egypt then lost the whole peninsula.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 5–6 June 1967, Wikidata 6 June. The place agrees.

summary.en: On 6 June 1967 one of the war's hardest battles is fought at Ammunition Hill, a Jordanian fortified position in East Jerusalem. On 7 June Moshe Dayan decides, without the government's approval, to take the Old City as the UN is expected to call a ceasefire. By that evening Israel holds almost the whole West Bank, and the military occupation begins.

title.en: Only one source for the Old City

text.en: The battle at Ammunition Hill on 6 June agrees with Wikidata. That the Old City and the West Bank were taken on 7 June rests only on Wikipedia's article on the Six-Day War.

summary.en: Syria accepts a ceasefire early on 9 June 1967, but the same morning Moshe Dayan gives the order to attack Syria. After two days of fighting on the Golan Heights the Syrian forces withdraw on 10 June. The ceasefire is signed the following day.

text.en: The fighting on the Golan Heights has no entry of its own with a date in Wikidata, so the event rests only on Wikipedia's article on the Six-Day War. The point is the Golan Heights according to Wikidata.

summary.en: On 6–25 October 1973 Israel fought a coalition of Arab states led by Egypt and Syria. The war began with a surprise attack on the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur, which that year coincided with the tenth day of Ramadan. In Israel it is called the Yom Kippur War and in the Arab world the October War or the Ramadan War.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the war lasted 6–25 October 1973, when the second ceasefire began. Wikidata gives the end date as 26 October.

intro.en: In the Six-Day War in 1967 Israel had taken the Sinai Peninsula from Egypt and about half of the Golan Heights from Syria. Israel's government decided in secret on 19 June 1967 to return the territories in exchange for peace, but according to the source the decision was never communicated to the Arab states. At the Khartoum summit in September 1967 the Arab states said no to peace, recognition and negotiations with Israel. The fighting continued in the so-called War of Attrition. Egypt and Syria wanted to regain the territories they had lost, and Egypt had been preparing the attack across the Suez Canal since 1968.

members.en: Egypt and Syria, with expeditionary forces from Saudi Arabia, Algeria, Jordan, Libya, Iraq, Kuwait, Tunisia, Morocco, Cuba and North Korea as well as Palestinian PLO groups in Lebanon. The Soviet Union sent large quantities of supplies.
Israel, with large deliveries of supplies from the United States.

outcome.en: After Egyptian and Syrian successes in the first days, Israel halted the attacks, advanced into Syria and crossed the Suez Canal. A ceasefire under UN Security Council Resolution 338 on 22 October broke down the next day, and the war ended with a second ceasefire on 25 October. By then Egypt held about 1,200 square kilometres east of the canal, and Israel about 1,600 square kilometres west of it and 500 square kilometres in Syria. The Arab world felt vindicated after the defeat in 1967, and Israel realised that its military superiority was not secure. This led to the Camp David Accords in 1978, when Israel returned Sinai, and to the peace treaty between Egypt and Israel, the first time an Arab country recognised Israel.

casualties.en: On the Israeli side 2,521 (Schiff) to 2,800 (Gawrych) died. On the Arab side a total of 8,000 (Gawrych) to 18,500 died, of whom 5,000–15,000 Egyptians and 3,000–3,500 Syrians. The figures are estimates and are given as ranges.

summary.en: On 6 October 1973 Egyptian forces cross the Suez Canal and break through the Bar Lev Line, Israel's fortifications along the canal in occupied Sinai. At the same time Syria attacks on the Golan Heights. Egypt had been preparing the attack since 1968, among other things with a deception operation.

caption.en: Egyptian vehicles crossing the Suez Canal on 7 October 1973. Photograph from Gammal Hammad's book on the fighting on the Egyptian front. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 6–9 October 1973 Israeli armoured units hold their positions against a much larger Syrian force on the northern Golan Heights. On the fourth day the Syrians withdraw, just as the Israeli defenders have almost collapsed. After the battle the place was given the name Valley of Tears.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 6–9 October 1973, and Wikidata gives 9 October, when the battle ended. The place agrees.

summary.en: On 15–17 October 1973 Israel and Egypt fight at an Egyptian agricultural research station east of the Suez Canal. Israel wanted to open a corridor to the canal so that it could build bridges and cross. After some of the hardest fighting of the war the Egyptians gave up control of the roads to the canal, and Israeli forces were able to cross to the western side.

After the ceasefire of 22 October has broken down, Israel tries to take the city of Suez on 24–25 October, but the armoured column is ambushed and the Israeli troops withdraw. It was the last battle of the war. On 25 October the second ceasefire began, which ended the war.
On 4 October 1957 Sputnik 1 is launched from what is today Baikonur. It is the first artificial satellite in orbit.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of space-age poster art from the 1950s, not a historical image.

summary.en: Apollo 11 is launched on 16 July 1969 and lands in the Sea of Tranquillity on the Moon on 20 July 1969.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of space-age poster art from the 1960s, not a historical image.

summary.en: A war on the Korean Peninsula between North Korea and South Korea and their allies. China and the Soviet Union supported North Korea, and UN forces under American leadership supported South Korea. About one million soldiers and an estimated 1.5–3 million civilians died. The fighting ended with an armistice in 1953, but no peace treaty has ever been signed.

intro.en: Korea had been a Japanese colony for 35 years. When the Second World War ended in 1945, the Soviet Union and the United States divided the country into two occupation zones at the 38th parallel, with plans for a future independent state. Because of political disagreement the zones formed their own governments in 1948: North Korea under Kim Il Sung in Pyongyang and South Korea under Syngman Rhee in Seoul. Both claimed to be the only legitimate government of all Korea. There were many border clashes, and Rhee's government put down communist uprisings on Jeju and in Yeosu–Suncheon. On 25 June 1950 North Korea attacked South Korea. The UN Security Council, where the Soviet Union's representative was absent, condemned the attack and called on member states to help repel it.

name.en: South Korea and the UN forces

members.en: South Korea and the UN Command with 21 countries, where the United States provided about 90 per cent of the soldiers. Among the others were the countries of the British Commonwealth.
North Korea, China (with the People's Volunteer Army from October 1950) and the Soviet Union (at most 26,000 men at one time).

outcome.en: The armistice of 27 July 1953 stopped the fighting, arranged the exchange of prisoners of war and created a four-kilometre-wide demilitarised zone along the front, near the 38th parallel. The border ended up roughly where it had been before the war: North Korea got the city of Kaesong and South Korea the city of Sokcho. South Korea never signed the armistice, and no peace treaty has ever been concluded. The conflict between the two states persists.

casualties.en: About one million soldiers and an estimated 1.5–3 million civilians died. On the side of South Korea and the UN about 210,000 soldiers died or went missing, among them 137,899 South Korean dead and 36,515 American dead or missing. On the side of North Korea and China about 600,000–630,000 died or went missing, among them 294,151–316,579 North Korean and 183,108–197,653 Chinese dead. According to South Korea's Ministry of National Defense, 373,599 South Korean civilians died and 387,744 went missing. The figures are estimates from different parties and are given as ranges.

summary.en: At four o'clock in the morning on 25 June 1950 North Korean forces cross the 38th parallel into South Korea, without a declaration of war. North Korea had prepared the attack for more than a year with secret support from the Soviet Union. Seoul is taken on 28 June. On 27 June US President Harry S. Truman orders air and naval forces to help South Korea.

The UN forces have been pushed back to a defensive line around the port of Pusan in south-eastern Korea. There about 140,000 soldiers, mainly South Korean, American and British, hold out against the North Korean army for six weeks, from 4 August to 18 September 1950. It is as far as North Korea gets in the war.

On 15 September 1950 UN forces under General Douglas MacArthur land at Inchon, far behind the front at Pusan. About 75,000 soldiers and 261 ships take part. The landing cuts the North Korean forces' lines of communication, and two weeks later the UN forces have retaken Seoul. The war turns.

caption.en: Lieutenant Baldomero Lopez leads his platoon over the sea wall at Red Beach in Inchon on 15 September 1950. Photograph by an unknown Marine Corps soldier, Naval History and Heritage Command. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The UN forces have advanced into North Korea and are approaching the Yalu River on the border with China. On 19 October 1950 the Chinese People's Volunteer Army crosses the Yalu. One of the first battles between Chinese and South Korean forces is fought around Onjong on 25–29 October, where Chinese units surprise and defeat parts of the South Korean army's II Corps.

On 27 November 1950 about 120,000 Chinese soldiers surprise about 30,000 men of the UN forces at the Chosin Reservoir in north-eastern Korea. For 17 days in severe cold the UN forces fight their way out of the encirclement to the port of Hungnam, where they are evacuated by sea. Both sides suffer heavy losses, also from the cold. The UN forces leave North Korea.

On 31 December 1950 Chinese forces attack the South Korean divisions along the 38th parallel. The American Eighth Army under Matthew Ridgway evacuates Seoul on 3 January 1951, and the city is taken by Chinese and North Korean forces. Two months later the UN forces retake Seoul.

On 27 July 1953 the armistice is signed at Panmunjom by the UN Command, the North Korean army and the Chinese volunteer forces. It takes effect at 22:00 the same day. The agreement creates the demilitarised zone between North and South Korea and arranges the exchange of prisoners of war. South Korea does not sign, and no peace treaty is ever concluded.

A war in Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia between North Vietnam and South Vietnam and their allies. The Soviet Union and China supported North Vietnam, and the United States and other anti-communist countries supported South Vietnam. The United States took part with its own combat troops from 1965 to 1973. An estimated 970,000–3 million Vietnamese soldiers and civilians died.

title.en: About the start of the war

text.en: There is no agreement on when the war began. In 1998 the US government counted the start from 1 November 1955, when the American Military Assistance Advisory Group in Vietnam was formed, and that year is used here. In 2012 President Barack Obama instead gave 12 January 1962, the first American combat mission in South Vietnam. Others count from December 1956, from the first battle between the NLF (Viet Cong) and the South Vietnamese army on 26 September 1959, or from 1960, 1954, 1950 or even 1945.

intro.en: After the First Indochina War, in which France was defeated, Vietnam's independence was confirmed at the Geneva Conference in 1954. The country was divided at the 17th parallel: the Viet Minh under Ho Chi Minh ruled North Vietnam, and Ngo Dinh Diem ruled South Vietnam, which received economic and military support from the United States. North Vietnam eventually supplied and directed the NLF (Viet Cong), a communist movement in the south that stepped up the guerrilla war from 1957. From 1958 North Vietnam built up the Ho Chi Minh Trail through Laos, and by 1961 at the latest it was secretly sending soldiers south. President John F. Kennedy increased the number of American military advisers. After the Gulf of Tonkin incident in 1964, Congress gave President Lyndon B. Johnson authority to increase the military presence without a declaration of war. The number of American soldiers rose to 184,000 in 1966 and 536,000 in 1969.

members.en: North Vietnam, the NLF (Viet Cong) and the Provisional Revolutionary Government in the south, the Pathet Lao in Laos and the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia, with support from the Soviet Union, China and North Korea.
South Vietnam, the United States, South Korea, Australia, Thailand, New Zealand and the Philippines, as well as the governments of Laos and the Khmer Republic in Cambodia.

outcome.en: North Vietnam won. From 1969 President Richard Nixon had the South Vietnamese army take over the fighting while American troops were withdrawn. After the Paris peace agreement of 27 January 1973 the last American forces left Vietnam, but the fighting continued. Saigon fell on 30 April 1975, and North and South Vietnam were formally unified on 2 July 1976. Laos and Cambodia also got communist governments in 1975.

casualties.en: Estimates differ widely. Wikipedia gives 970,000–3 million Vietnamese soldiers and civilians killed. The Vietnamese government has stated 849,018 soldiers killed on the side of North Vietnam and the NLF and about 2 million civilians killed, while American estimates for 1964–1974 give 666,000–950,765 killed on the same side. In Cambodia 275,000–310,000 people died and in Laos 20,000–62,000 in the civil wars there. About 58,000 American soldiers died. The figures are estimates and are given as ranges.

summary.en: On 2 August 1964 an American destroyer gathering intelligence near the coast of North Vietnam clashes with three North Vietnamese torpedo boats. On the night of 4 August two American destroyers report a new attack, but later inquiries showed that the attack never took place. Congress passes the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, which gives President Johnson authority to deploy American forces.

The first major battle between the US Army and the North Vietnamese Army is fought in the Central Highlands on 14–18 November 1965. It is the first major airmobile assault with helicopters, and the first time B-52 bombers are used to support troops on the ground. The battle becomes a pattern for the war: the Americans rely on firepower from the air, and the North Vietnamese fight at very close quarters.

On 21 January 1968 North Vietnamese forces, two to three divisions, surround the American Marine Corps base at Khe Sanh. For five months the base is shelled daily, and the United States responds with extensive bombing from the air. The fighting lasts until 9 July 1968, and both sides claim to have won.

During the Vietnamese New Year, on 30–31 January 1968, the North Vietnamese Army and the NLF launch a surprise attack on more than 100 cities in South Vietnam, among them the capital Saigon. The expected popular uprising fails to materialise, and the attacks are beaten back. The offensive, which continues in three phases until September, becomes a military defeat for North Vietnam but reduces support for the war in the United States.

caption.en: Old and young flee the fighting in Hue during the Tet Offensive and make their way to the south bank of the Perfume River despite a blown-up bridge. Photograph from USIA, 1968, in the US National Archives. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: From 29 April 1970 South Vietnamese forces, and from 1 May American forces, enter eastern Cambodia. The aim is the roughly 40,000 soldiers of the North Vietnamese Army and the NLF who have bases across the border. The campaign follows the deposition of Prince Norodom Sihanouk by General Lon Nol. The American operations last until 30 June and the South Vietnamese ones until 22 July. The leadership of the North Vietnamese forces escapes.

text.en: Wikidata's entry has no place, so the place could not be compared with a second, independent source. The information comes from Wikipedia.

summary.en: On 8 February 1971 the South Vietnamese army enters south-eastern Laos to strike at the Ho Chi Minh Trail, North Vietnam's supply route to the south. The United States contributes air power, artillery and logistics, but under law American ground troops may not enter Laos. The offensive collapses against fierce resistance and ends on 25 March 1971.

On 29 April 1975 the North Vietnamese Army and the NLF begin the final attack on Saigon, the capital of South Vietnam. Thousands of civilians and Americans are evacuated. On 30 April President Dương Văn Minh surrenders, and the NLF flag is raised over the presidential palace. South Vietnam ceases to exist, and the war is over.

From 28 December 1958 rebels under Che Guevara take the city of Santa Clara from General Fulgencio Batista's regime. Within twelve hours of the city's fall, Batista flees Cuba, and Fidel Castro's forces take power. The battle decides the Cuban Revolution, and the sources date it to 1 January 1959.
Hamida Djandoubi is executed by guillotine in Marseille on 10 September 1977. He becomes the last person to be executed in France before the death penalty is abolished in 1981.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of a documentary newspaper illustration from the 1970s, not a historical image.

summary.en: The film Star Wars premieres in a small number of cinemas in the United States on 25 May 1977 and quickly becomes an unexpected box-office success.

caption.en: A cinema in California advertises Star Wars, 1977. Photograph by Michael Dorausch. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

summary.en: At midnight between 14 and 15 August 1947 British rule in India ends. An act of the British Parliament divides British India into two independent states, India and Pakistan, which then also includes present-day Bangladesh. Independence was the goal of a long freedom movement, known for non-violent resistance and civil disobedience under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi. In New Delhi Jawaharlal Nehru gives his speech about the tryst with destiny and becomes India's first prime minister. The partition is followed by mass violence: between 12 and 20 million people are driven from their homes, and estimates of the number of dead range from 200,000 to 2 million.

caption.en: Jawaharlal Nehru speaks from the Red Fort on India's Independence Day, 15 August 1947. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 6 March 1957 the British colony of the Gold Coast becomes independent under the name Ghana, with Kwame Nkrumah as prime minister. He tells the people that Africans can manage their own affairs and that Ghana is free for ever. The road there ran through a nationalist movement after the Second World War: the unrest in Accra in 1948, Nkrumah's party the CPP from 1949 and the campaign of positive action with strikes and non-violent resistance, which got him imprisoned but also won him the people's support. Ghana is one of the first countries south of the Sahara to become free from European colonial rule.

caption.en: The US delegation at Ghana's independence celebrations in 1957, with Finance Minister K. A. Gbedemah. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: During 1960, 17 African colonies become independent: 14 from France, two from the United Kingdom and one from Belgium. The number of independent countries in Africa rises from nine to 26. First is Cameroon on 1 January, followed by, among others, Togo, Madagascar, Somalia, both Congos and Nigeria on 1 October. It is the high point of the African independence movements. In the same year the armed struggle against apartheid begins in South Africa, and in the Congo Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba is overthrown, and is then tortured and executed. In December the UN General Assembly adopts a declaration that all peoples have the right to self-determination.

On 10 December 1948 the UN General Assembly, meeting at the Palais de Chaillot in Paris, adopts the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. 48 countries vote yes, no country votes no and eight abstain. The committee that wrote the declaration was chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt.

caption.en: Eleanor Roosevelt with a poster of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Lake Success, New York, November 1949, a year after the declaration was adopted. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: On 1 October 1949 the chairman of the Communist Party, Mao Zedong, proclaims the People's Republic of China from the Gate of Heavenly Peace (Tiananmen) in Beijing. The communists have by then taken control of most of the mainland, and the government of the Republic of China has withdrawn to the island of Taiwan in December of the same year.

On 22 May 1960 southern Chile is struck by the strongest earthquake ever measured, with a magnitude of 9.4–9.6. The earthquake and the tsunamis kill between about 1,000 and 6,000 people. The tsunami crosses the Pacific to Hawaii, where 61 people die in the city of Hilo, and to Japan.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 22 May 1960 and Wikidata 21 May 1960. The magnitude is given as 9.4–9.6 in Wikipedia and as 9.5 in Wikidata.

caption.en: Earthquake damage to wooden houses in Valdivia, Chile, 1960. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin is launched in the spacecraft Vostok 1 from the Baikonur Cosmodrome. He becomes the first human in space and the first to travel a full orbit around the Earth. The flight takes 108 minutes from launch to landing.

caption.en: Yuri Gagarin, 12 April 1961. Licence: CC BY 4.0 (Mos.ru).

summary.en: In October 1962 the United States and the Soviet Union are set against each other after the Soviet Union has placed nuclear missiles in Cuba. The crisis is resolved diplomatically: the Soviet Union removes the missiles under UN supervision, and the United States promises not to invade Cuba and quietly removes its own nuclear missiles from Turkey and Italy. Afterwards the two countries get a hotline for crisis situations.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the crisis lasted 16–28 October 1962 and Wikidata 14–28 October 1962.

caption.en: One of the first reconnaissance photographs of missile sites under construction in Cuba, shown to President Kennedy on the morning of 16 October 1962. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 11 September 1973 the Chilean military overthrows the socialist president Salvador Allende. The presidential palace La Moneda in Santiago is bombed, and Allende dies in the palace. It is generally regarded as suicide, but the circumstances are disputed. A military junta under General Augusto Pinochet takes power, and the military dictatorship lasts until 1990.

caption.en: The bombing of the presidential palace La Moneda in Santiago on 11 September 1973. Licence: CC BY 3.0 CL.

summary.en: In October 1977 the hospital cook Ali Maow Maalin falls ill in the port town of Merca in southern Somalia. He is the last known person to be infected with smallpox outside a laboratory. The World Health Organization (WHO) then declares the disease eradicated. Smallpox is the only human disease to have been eradicated. The last known death occurred in 1978 in a laboratory in Birmingham, England.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on Ali Maow Maalin says that WHO declared smallpox eradicated on 26 October 1979. The article on smallpox says that WHO certified the eradication in May 1980.

caption.en: Smallpox virus under an electron microscope, magnified about 370,000 times. Image from 1975. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 25 April 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge describe the double helix of the DNA molecule in the journal Nature. The discovery was made on 28 February of the same year. The article was also based on unpublished work by Rosalind Franklin, Maurice Wilkins and others at King's College London. Watson, Crick and Wilkins receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962.

caption.en: The model of the DNA molecule that Crick and Watson built in 1953, photographed in the Science Museum in London in the present day. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In March 1958 Charles David Keeling of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography begins measuring the air's carbon dioxide content at the Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii. The first measurement gives 313 parts per million. The series of measurements, known as the Keeling Curve, shows that the level is rising steadily, and ever faster, because of the burning of fossil fuels. In November 2018 the level was 406 parts per million.

caption.en: Charles David Keeling and John Chin at the Mauna Loa Observatory in 1997, almost 40 years after the first measurements. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 26 July 1953 Fidel Castro and his brother Raúl attack the Moncada Barracks, and it becomes the start of an uprising against Fulgencio Batista's regime. At the turn of the year 1958–1959 Batista is overthrown and flees the country, and Castro's 26th of July Movement takes over the government. In October 1965 the movement becomes Cuba's Communist Party.

On 13 August 1961 the East German government begins building the Berlin Wall. The regime calls it an anti-fascist protective rampart, but the main purpose is to stop East Germans from fleeing to the West. The Wall and the border around West Berlin become 155 kilometres long. Between 136 and more than 200 people are killed by East German authorities at the border before the Wall is opened in 1989.

caption.en: East German construction workers build the Berlin Wall on 20 November 1961. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 28 August 1963 about 250,000 people gather in Washington, D.C. for jobs and freedom and for civil rights. At the Lincoln Memorial Martin Luther King Jr. gives the speech “I Have a Dream”. The march contributes to the passing of the Civil Rights Act in 1964 and the Voting Rights Act in 1965.

caption.en: The leaders of the march walk from the Washington Monument towards the Lincoln Memorial on 28 August 1963. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In May 1966 the chairman of the Communist Party, Mao Zedong, launches the Cultural Revolution. He urges young people to “bombard the headquarters”, and many form groups of Red Guards all over China. Estimates of how many are killed vary from hundreds of thousands to millions. The Cultural Revolution ends when Mao dies in 1976 and the Gang of Four are arrested.

caption.en: A quotation from Mao Zedong's Little Red Book, painted on a house wall in Zhuji during the Cultural Revolution. Present-day photo from 2005. Licence: CC BY 1.0.

summary.en: On 21 April 1960 President Juscelino Kubitschek inaugurated Brasília as Brazil's new capital in place of Rio de Janeiro. The city was built in 41 months on the Brazilian highlands. It was planned by Lúcio Costa, and the architect Oscar Niemeyer designed most of the public buildings.

On 6 August 1962 Jamaica became independent from the United Kingdom. The island had gained increasing self-government and from 1958 was part of the West Indies Federation, but in a referendum in 1961 a narrow majority voted to leave it. Jamaica became a parliamentary monarchy and remained in the Commonwealth.

The forest-covered mountain Mount Lamington had not been recognised as a volcano until it had a devastating eruption in January 1951. The eruption began on the night of 18 January, and three days later a large part of the mountain's northern side was blown away. Pyroclastic flows and ash killed about 3,000 people, and more than 5,000 were left homeless.

text.en: The source gives about 3,000 dead but also mentions a figure of 3,466 dead.

summary.en: On Christmas Eve 1953, at 22.21, a railway bridge over the Whangaehu River at Tangiwai collapsed as an express train drove onto it. The locomotive and the first six carriages ended up in the river, and 151 people died. Only minutes earlier a mudflow, a lahar, from the crater lake of the volcano Ruapehu had destroyed one of the bridge's piers. It is New Zealand's worst railway accident.

The Summer Olympics were held in Melbourne on 22 November–8 December 1956. They were the first Olympic Games in the Southern Hemisphere and in Oceania, and the first outside Europe and North America. The equestrian events were held in Stockholm in June, because Australia's quarantine rules kept the horses out. Nine countries boycotted the Games, among other reasons because of the Suez Crisis and the Soviet invasion of Hungary.

On 1 January 1962 Western Samoa became independent, after New Zealand, through an act from November 1961, had ended its trusteeship. New Zealand had governed the territory since German Samoa was conquered in 1914, and the independence movement Mau had long protested without violence. Samoa became the first independent country in the Pacific.

Between 1966 and 1996 France tested nuclear weapons on the atolls of Moruroa and Fangataufa in the Tuamotu Islands, about 1,250 km south-east of Tahiti. The tests prompted international protests, especially in 1974 and 1995. How many tests were carried out on Moruroa is given differently, 175 or 181.

On 23 August 1966 about 200 Gurindji stockmen, domestic workers and their families left the Wave Hill cattle station under the leadership of Vincent Lingiari. What was at first seen as a strike for better conditions was a demand to get back part of the Gurindji people's land. On 16 August 1975 Prime Minister Gough Whitlam symbolically handed land back to them. The event led to the Aboriginal Land Rights Act in 1976.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the strike began on 23 August 1966 and lasted until 16 August 1975. Wikidata gives 26 August 1966 as the start and April 1971 as the end.

summary.en: On 10 October 1970 Fiji became independent after 96 years as a British Crown colony. At a conference in London in April 1970 agreement had been reached on an electoral system that divided the seats in parliament between indigenous Fijians, Indo-Fijians and other groups. Queen Elizabeth II was head of state until Fiji was proclaimed a republic in 1987, after two military coups.

On 20 October 1973 Queen Elizabeth II inaugurated the opera house at Bennelong Point in Sydney Harbour. The Danish architect Jørn Utzon had won the architectural competition in 1957, but the building ran over both time and budget and Utzon resigned. An Australian team under Peter Hall completed the building. Since 2007 the opera house has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

On 24 December 1974 Cyclone Tracy turned towards Darwin in northern Australia. After 22:00 the damage became severe, with wind gusts of 217 km/h before the instruments broke. 66 people died, and more than 70 per cent of the city's buildings were destroyed. Over 30,000 people were evacuated, and the city was then rebuilt under stricter building codes.

On 16 September 1975 Papua New Guinea became independent from Australia. Eastern New Guinea had been divided between Germany and the United Kingdom in the 1880s. After the First World War Australia received the League of Nations mandate over the German part, and from 1949 Australia administered Papua and New Guinea together.

The United States launches its first satellite, Explorer 1, on a Juno I rocket from Cape Canaveral in Florida. The Soviet Union had launched Sputnik 1 and Sputnik 2 the year before. Explorer 1 becomes the first spacecraft to detect the Van Allen belt, a radiation belt around the Earth.

text.en: The launch took place on the evening of 31 January 1958 in local time on the US East Coast, which was 1 February in Greenwich Mean Time (GMT). The date given here is 1 February, as in Wikidata.

summary.en: On 16 June 1963 Valentina Tereshkova is launched in the spacecraft Vostok 6, the first spaceflight with a woman on board. She flies alone, orbits the Earth 48 times and spends almost three days in space. It is the last flight of the Vostok programme.

France launches its first satellite, Astérix, on a Diamant rocket from the Hammaguir launch site in Algeria. France becomes the third country to launch a satellite on its own rocket. The main purpose is to test the rocket, and the satellite is still orbiting the Earth.

Japan launches its first satellite, Ohsumi, from the Kagoshima Space Center on the Ohsumi peninsula. The Lambda 4S rocket was developed at the University of Tokyo. Japan becomes the fourth country to place a satellite in orbit on its own.

China launches its first satellite, Dong Fang Hong 1, on a Long March 1 rocket from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center. The satellite weighs 173 kilograms, more than other countries' first satellites. It broadcasts the song "The East Is Red" for 20 days.

The Soviet Union launches Salyut 1, the world's first space station. The crew of Soyuz 11 stays on board for 23 days, but they die during the return to Earth when a valve fails. The mission is then ended, and the station burns up in the atmosphere in October 1971.

The United Kingdom launches the satellite Prospero on its own Black Arrow rocket from Woomera in South Australia. It is the first British satellite launched on a British rocket, and the last: the Black Arrow programme had already been cancelled. Britain's first satellite in orbit, Ariel 1, had been launched on a US rocket in 1962.

India's first satellite, Aryabhata, is launched from Kapustin Yar in the Soviet Union. It was built by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and is named after the astronomer Aryabhata. The Soviet Union launches it under an agreement in which India in return lets Soviet ships use Indian ports.

The European Space Agency (ESA) is founded when the two organisations ESRO and ELDO are merged. Ten countries are members from the start: Belgium, Denmark, France, West Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and the United Kingdom. Its headquarters are in Paris.

text.en: Wikipedia says that ESA was founded with the ESA Convention in 1975, and Wikidata gives 30 May 1975. The convention only came into force in 1980, when all the countries had ratified it.

summary.en: The first Ariane rocket is launched from the space centre at Kourou in French Guiana. Ariane 1 was developed for the European Space Agency (ESA) and is the first launcher built mainly to send commercial satellites into orbit. The French president Valéry Giscard d'Estaing presses the launch button himself.

New Zealand's parliament passes the Statute of Westminster Adoption Act, which receives royal assent on 25 November 1947. The country thereby adopts the Statute of Westminster, the British act of 1931 that gave the dominions full sovereignty, as the last dominion to do so. At the time it was seen as a necessary constitutional step and not as a change in the relationship with Britain, but today it is regarded as an important step towards independence. The act was replaced by the Constitution Act 1986.

text.en: Store norske leksikon writes that the country became fully independent of Britain in 1947. Lex writes in one place that the country's status was established by the Statute of Westminster in December 1931. The date of the royal assent comes only from Wikipedia.

summary.en: After years of growing Māori protest over unresolved breaches of the Treaty of Waitangi, Parliament passes the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975. The act establishes the Waitangi Tribunal (Te Rōpū Whakamana i te Tiriti o Waitangi), a permanent commission of inquiry. At first it could only hear claims about events after 1975, but in 1985 its jurisdiction was extended back to 1840. The Tribunal's findings are as a rule recommendations that do not bind the Crown.

text.en: Wikidata dates the act to 10 October 1975. Wikipedia gives only the year, so only the year is shown here.

summary.en: With Denmark's new constitution in 1953, Greenland became part of Denmark instead of a colony and was given two members in the Folketing. Greenlanders were not allowed to vote in the referendum on the constitution.

text.en: According to Lex, the prevailing view is that the colonial era ended in 1953, but there is also a view that the colonial relationship continued in practice, since all laws for Greenland were still made in Copenhagen.

summary.en: After a referendum in January 1979, Greenland was granted home rule on 1 May the same year. A parliament of its own, the Landsting, could now make laws on parts of society. The same year the capital Godthåb was officially renamed Nuuk.

On 3 December 1967 the surgeon Christiaan Barnard performed the first human-to-human heart transplant, at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town. The patient, 54-year-old Louis Washkansky, received the heart of the accident victim Denise Darvall. He survived the operation but died after 18 days of pneumonia, possibly because of the drugs that suppressed his immune system.

At 11.30 a.m. on 29 May 1953 Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary reached the summit of the world’s highest mountain. They belonged to the ninth expedition to attempt the summit, a British expedition led by John Hunt, and it was the first confirmed ascent. George Mallory had disappeared on the mountain during an earlier expedition in 1924. Sherpas carried loads to the higher camps. The news reached London on the morning of 2 June, the day of Queen Elizabeth II’s coronation.

On 14 October 1956 B. R. Ambedkar converted to Buddhism at Deekshabhoomi in Nagpur, more than 20 years after he had declared his intention to do so. He had written that Buddhism was the only way to equality for those regarded as untouchables. At the same ceremony a very large number of his followers, mainly Dalits, also converted, and two days later more than 300,000 more in Chandrapur. Ambedkar inspired many further mass conversions, and Deekshabhoomi became a place of pilgrimage.

text.en: The number who converted at the ceremony in Nagpur differs: about 365,000 according to the article on the Dalit Buddhist movement and about 400,000 according to the article on Deekshabhoomi, which says that figure is Ambedkar’s own.

summary.en: On 23 January 1960 the bathyscaphe Trieste reached the bottom of the Challenger Deep, the deepest part of the Mariana Trench and the deepest point on Earth’s seabed. It was the first time a crewed vessel had got there. On board were the Swiss oceanographer Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh, a lieutenant in the US Navy. Trieste had been designed by Jacques’s father Auguste Piccard and built in Italy, and the dive was the goal of the US Navy’s Project Nekton near Guam.

On 14 September 1960 Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela founded the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, OPEC, in Baghdad. By cooperating, the oil-producing countries wanted to influence the world oil market together. Its membership has changed since then, and according to the source most of the world’s proven oil reserves are estimated to lie in OPEC countries.

From 11 October 1962 to 8 December 1965 the bishops of the Catholic Church met in four sessions in St. Peter’s Basilica. The council was convened by Pope John XXIII and concluded under Paul VI. Nearly 2,500 bishops took part at some point, along with non-Catholic observers. They adopted sixteen documents, including on the liturgy, the Church’s relationship with the modern world, religious freedom and other religions. The liturgy, which for centuries had been celebrated almost entirely in Latin, could now be celebrated in the people’s own languages.

From 15 January to 12 February 1977 the Second World Black and African Festival of Arts and Culture was held in Lagos. The festival showcased African music, art, literature, drama, dance and religion. Around 16,000 participants from 56 African nations and countries of the African diaspora performed, among them Miriam Makeba, Franco Luambo Makiadi, Gilberto Gil and Stevie Wonder, and around 500,000 spectators came. It was the largest pan-African gathering up to then. The National Theatre in Iganmu was built for the festival.

On 9 January 1960 Egypt began building the Aswan High Dam on the Nile, with help from the Soviet Union, which also sent technicians and heavy machinery. The dam was completed on 21 July 1970. It was meant to control the Nile floods and provide electricity and water. Behind the dam Lake Nasser formed, flooding much of Lower Nubia, and 100,000–120,000 people were resettled in Sudan and Egypt. The temples of Abu Simbel were moved up to the shore in UNESCO’s campaign to save the monuments of Nubia. When the dam first reached peak output in 1970 it produced around half of Egypt’s electricity, and the country’s irrigated area grew by a third. The silt now settles in the lake, and the dam is blamed for erosion of the Nile Delta coast and for soil salinity.

From the late 1960s the Sahel, the belt south of the Sahara, was struck by a long drought. It was most severe in 1968–1974 and again in the early and mid-1980s. Famine and displacement hit hard in, among others, Mauritania, Mali, Chad, Niger and Upper Volta, today Burkina Faso. During the drought of 1968–1973 up to 100,000 people and a third of the livestock died. For a long time the drought was thought to be caused mainly by overgrazing, deforestation and poor land management. Later research has instead pointed to changing sea surface temperatures and to air pollution from Eurasia and North America. Since the 1980s summer rainfall in the Sahel has been increasing again.

text.en: The source describes a drought period from the 1960s to the 1980s with two peaks, 1968–1974 and the early and mid-1980s. The death toll of up to 100,000 refers to the drought of 1968–1973; elsewhere the source says that famine killed 100,000 people from the late 1960s to the early 1980s. The end year 1985 is approximate.

summary.en: On 16 June 1976 Black schoolchildren in Soweto, South Africa, came out to protest against a decree of 1974 that required Black schools to teach in Afrikaans and English in equal measure. According to one estimate about 20,000 students took part. The police opened fire, and among the first to be killed were 15-year-old Hastings Ndlovu and 12-year-old Hector Pieterson. Sam Nzima’s photograph of Hector Pieterson became the symbol of the uprising. The violence in Soweto died down on 18 June, but the unrest spread across the country. The death tolls differ: the government first reported 23 students killed, other figures speak of 176 dead on the first day alone, the Cillié Commission counted 575 dead by February 1977, and The Times more than 700 across the country by the end of 1976. Today 16 June is a public holiday in South Africa, Youth Day.

On 26 August 1976 an outbreak of an unknown disease began in the small village of Yambuku in Zaire, today the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The Congolese doctor Jean-Jacques Muyembe-Tamfum took a blood sample from a Belgian nun, and with that sample Peter Piot identified a previously unknown virus. Piot concluded that the nuns had unknowingly started the epidemic by giving unnecessary vitamin injections to pregnant women, with syringes and needles that were not sterilised. In Zaire 318 people fell ill and 280 died, 88 per cent. In the same year, from June to November, the first known outbreak, in Nzara in present-day South Sudan had infected 284 and killed 151. The virus was named after the Ebola River.

The civil war in Angola began when the country became independent from Portugal in November 1975 and lasted, with interruptions, until 2002. It was a power struggle between two former liberation movements: the communist MPLA, helped by Cuban soldiers and supported by the Soviet Union, and the anti-communist UNITA, backed by the United States and South Africa. The war is widely seen as a Cold War proxy conflict. The major fighting came in three rounds, 1975–1991, 1992–1994 and 1998–2002. By the time the MPLA won in 2002, 500,000–800,000 people had died and over a million had been displaced within the country, and land mines still injure and kill civilians.

intro.en: From 1961 the FNLA and the MPLA waged guerrilla war against Portuguese colonial rule. After the Carnation Revolution in Lisbon in 1974, the Angolan movements signed the Alvor Accords on 15 January 1975. In July 1975 the MPLA violently forced the FNLA out of Luanda, and UNITA withdrew to its stronghold in the south. On 23 October South African troops entered southern Angola in support of the FNLA and UNITA, and Zaire sent troops to support the FNLA. On 11 November 1975 the MPLA leader Agostinho Neto proclaimed the People’s Republic of Angola, while UNITA and the FNLA proclaimed republics of their own.

members.en: The People’s Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA), a movement based in and around Luanda and drawn mainly from the Mbundu people, led by Agostinho Neto and from 1979 by José Eduardo dos Santos. It was helped by Cuban soldiers and supported by the Soviet Union.

The National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA), drawn mainly from the Ovimbundu people of the Bié Plateau and led by Jonas Savimbi. It was backed by the United States and South Africa. The FNLA, rooted among the Bakongo people in the north, fought on the same side at first but played almost no role in the civil war.

outcome.en: The Bicesse Accords of 31 May 1991 led to elections in 1992, but the fighting soon began again. The Lusaka Protocol was signed on 31 October 1994, and in December 1998 the war flared up anew. Government troops killed Jonas Savimbi on 22 February 2002 in Moxico province, and on 13 March the government halted its military operations. On 4 April 2002 the military commanders signed an addendum to the Lusaka Protocol in Luena. UNITA became a political party and demobilised its army in August 2002.

casualties.en: Between 500,000 and 800,000 dead and over a million internally displaced by 2002. Between 1975 and 1989 alone, according to the source, more than 500,000 Angolans were killed, in combat or indirectly through bombing, land mines and starvation.

summary.en: In the early 1960s the Soviet Union diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, which fed the Aral Sea, to irrigate the desert and grow cotton. The Aral Sea had been the fourth-largest lake in the world, with an area of 68,000 km², and now began to shrink. By 2007 it had fallen to 10 per cent of its original size and split into four lakes. In 2010 UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon called it one of the planet's worst environmental disasters.

text.en: The source says in one place that the Aral Sea began to shrink in the 1950s and 1960s, and in another that it began in the 1960s, when the rivers were diverted.

summary.en: On 2 February 1971 an international treaty to conserve wetlands and use them sustainably, especially as a habitat for waterfowl, was signed in the city of Ramsar in Iran. The treaty has a list of wetlands of international importance. In February 2025 there were 2,531 such Ramsar sites, covering more than 2.6 million km².

From 5 to 16 June 1972 the UN Conference on the Human Environment was held in Stockholm. Sweden had proposed the conference in 1968, and the UN General Assembly decided in 1969 to hold it. The Canadian Maurice Strong led it. The Soviet Union and the other Warsaw Pact countries boycotted the conference because East Germany was not allowed to take part. The conference led to the creation of the UN Environment Programme, UNEP, with its headquarters in Nairobi, Kenya, the first UN agency based in a developing country.

On 3 March 1973 the text of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species, CITES, was finalised at a meeting in Washington of representatives of 80 countries. The treaty is meant to ensure that international trade in wild animals and plants does not threaten the survival of the species. It entered into force on 1 July 1975, after ten countries had ratified it. Today CITES gives varying degrees of protection to more than 40,900 species.

In 1975 the Australian government passed a law on the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park. The law created an authority for the park and defined which acts were prohibited on the reef. The authority manages the park with tools such as zoning, plans, agreements with Traditional Owners, research and monitoring.

In 1977 Professor Wangari Maathai founded the Green Belt Movement together with the National Council of Women of Kenya. The first tree planting took place in Nairobi on 5 June 1977. The movement linked women's poverty to degraded land and enabled women to plant trees and earn their own income. Since the start more than 51 million trees have been planted, and in 2004 Maathai received the Nobel Peace Prize for the work.

In 1968 the Catholic bishops of Latin America met in Medellín in Colombia to apply the Second Vatican Council to Latin America. Its 16 documents dealt with the Church in a changing Latin America, with a focus on the poor and oppressed. The bishops said that the Church should take “a preferential option for the poor” and approved base communities in which the poor could learn to read by reading the Bible. They held that poverty and hunger could be prevented.

Operation Condor was cooperation between the right-wing dictatorships of the Southern Cone of South America to persecute left-wing sympathisers, with intelligence operations and assassinations, including across borders. On 25 November 1975 the intelligence chiefs of Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay and Uruguay met the head of Chile's secret police in Santiago; Brazil signed in June 1976. The United States financed the covert operations. The cooperation ended when the Argentine junta fell in 1983. How many were killed is disputed: estimates range from about 50,000 to 80,000 dead, and according to one of them about 400,000 people were imprisoned.

text.en: Wikipedia says that Operation Condor formally existed from 1975 to 1983. Wikidata gives 1989 as the end year. The number of dead is disputed because the operation was secret; Wikipedia gives 60,000–80,000 dead in its infobox, at least 60,000 dead in the text, and in another estimate 50,000 killed, 30,000 disappeared and 400,000 imprisoned.
